claims.text: Compositional disorder in high-entropy alloys produces high intrinsic lattice friction.
Coherent multilayer interfaces act as barriers to dislocation nucleation.
Coherent multilayer interfaces act as barriers to dislocation propagation.
The combination of intrinsic lattice friction and coherent interfaces enhances the creep resistance of HEA multilayer coatings.
The proposed coating consists of chemically disordered, single-phase solid-solution HEA layers.
Interfaces between the proposed layers are coherent or semi-coherent.
An alternating multilayer coating should be compared with a monolithic HEA coating under identical loading conditions.
Creep is measurable under sustained loading at elevated temperature below phase-transformation limits.
Multilayer interfaces and composition-induced lattice distortion are localized obstacles to dislocation motion.
Interfaces impede dislocation glide and climb by acting as energy barriers.
Time-dependent deformation in the relevant HEA coatings is governed by dislocation processes.
Random local chemical environments increase the activation energy for dislocation motion.
The interface barriers and increased lattice friction jointly reduce the accumulation of creep strain.
Multilayer HEA coatings will have a significantly lower creep rate than comparable monolithic HEA coatings.
Multilayer HEA coatings will accumulate less plastic strain than comparable monolithic HEA coatings.
The comparison baseline is a monolithic HEA coating with similar overall composition and microstructure but no multilayer architecture.
The proposed effect requires a layer thickness that maintains coherent interfaces.
The proposed effect applies only where phase changes and microstructural instabilities do not occur.
The magnitude of creep-rate reduction and the relative contributions of interface and lattice resistance are unquantified and may depend on layer thickness and processing.
A lack of statistically significant creep reduction or distinguishable interface-dislocation interactions would falsify the hypothesis.
